title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media, a deepfake video and voice presented as a sitting chief minister on a live WhatsApp video call. The failure sits at the point of contact, not inside any system the victim was using: a consumer messaging app carried the call, and nothing in that channel verified who was on the other end. The fraud depended on the target treating an unverified face and voice as proof of identity, and the demands that followed, including a second caller claiming to be a CBI officer, were a script built on that assumed authority.

Catching it would have required verification outside the call itself, through an official channel independent of the caller, or detection of the synthetic video and audio before or during the call. Neither the platform nor the recipient had a check of that kind available. The escalation from an aid offer to a PIN problem to a fine is a social engineering sequence, and each step worked because the first identity claim was never tested.

What is not established is who made the deepfake, what tools were used, or whether anyone will be charged, since a case registered under the Information Technology Act is an investigation and not a finding. The account rests on a single outlet's report.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9 from 7986304658. The caller used an AI generated deepfake video and voice to pose as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and offered financial aid. The fraudster said Giri would get Rs 11 lakh, later claimed Rs 5 lakh was allotted, and asked for processing and other payments. This was the city's first reported case of its kind.

Giri paid Rs 5,000, then Rs 18,000 after being told his PIN was locked. A person claiming to be a CBI officer named Thakur demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Fearing loss of earlier payments, Giri transferred money through a digital payment app, losing over Rs 1.04 lakh. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been duped. He contacted cybercrime helpline 1930 and Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act. Police urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on them.
